original_question: Characterize exactly which C_0-semigroups on L^p-spaces admit a loose dilation within the class of all L^p-spaces. Here a semigroup (T(t))_{t >= 0} has a loose dilation in a class X if there exist a space Y in X, bounded linear maps J: X -> Y and Q: Y -> X, and a bounded C_0-group (U(t))_{t in R} on Y such that T(t) = Q U(t) J for every t >= 0.
target_in_paper: Problem 4.4.1 in §4.4 (“Notes & Open Problems”): “Let p ∈ (1,∞) \ {2}. Characterize those bounded semigroups on L^p that have a loose dilation in the class of all L^p-spaces.” ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))
correct_elements: Your draft has the right target topic and is very close to the paper’s actual open problem: it asks for a characterization of semigroups on L^p-spaces admitting a loose dilation, and your definition of “loose dilation” matches Definition 1.4.1(ii) in substance. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))
missing_details: The paper fixes a single exponent p with p ∈ (1,∞) \ {2}; it is not asking for a simultaneous characterization across all p, and it explicitly excludes p = 2. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))

The official problem is about bounded semigroups on L^p, i.e. bounded C_0-semigroups, not arbitrary C_0-semigroups. Your draft omits the boundedness hypothesis. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))

To be stand-alone, the underlying space should be written as an arbitrary L^p(Ω), and the dilation space should be another L^p(Ω') with the same exponent p; “the class of all L^p-spaces” in this context means varying the measure space, not the exponent. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))

If you keep the question self-contained, you should state explicitly that bounded means sup_{t≥0} ||T(t)|| < ∞. This is implicit in the paper’s wording “bounded semigroups.” ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))

Your draft is slightly broader than the paper because it does not reflect the nearby context that the strict-dilation case is already characterized: Theorem 4.2.13 settles strict dilations on L^p via r-contractivity, and Problem 4.4.1 asks only for the loose-dilation analogue. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))
The paper works in the usual complex Banach-space/L^p-space setting, which your draft leaves implicit. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))
refined_question: Fix p ∈ (1,∞) \ {2}. Let (T(t))_{t≥0} be a bounded C_0-semigroup on a complex L^p-space L^p(Ω). Characterize precisely those semigroups for which there exist another L^p-space L^p(Ω'), bounded linear maps J: L^p(Ω) → L^p(Ω') and Q: L^p(Ω') → L^p(Ω), and a bounded C_0-group (U(t))_{t∈ℝ} on L^p(Ω') such that T(t) = Q U(t) J for every t ≥ 0; equivalently, characterize the bounded C_0-semigroups on L^p(Ω) that admit a loose dilation in the class of all L^p-spaces with the same exponent p.
justification: The nearest official formulation is exactly Problem 4.4.1 in §4.4. The surrounding sentences immediately before it say that Theorem 4.2.13 already characterizes semigroups on L^p with a strict dilation in the class of all L^p-spaces, so the unresolved issue is specifically the loose-dilation analogue, not a broader dilation problem. Definition 1.4.1(ii) supplies the exact meaning of “loose dilation.” In nearby background, Proposition 1.4.2 and Theorem 1.4.3 explain why this question matters: on UMD-spaces, loose dilations force a bounded H^∞-calculus of angle at most π/2, and angle strictly less than π/2 yields a loose dilation to L^2([0,1];X). Hence your draft is mathematically on target, but to be fully paper-faithful it must add the fixed exponent p ∈ (1,∞) \ {2}, the boundedness assumption on the semigroup, and the fact that the dilation ranges over L^p-spaces with the same exponent p. ([d-nb.info](https://d-nb.info/1064939813/34))
